title: Transfer of Ownership and Delivery of Goods
outcomes: Apply Sections 18 to 25 to decide when property in goods passes from seller to buyer — specific, unascertained, approval and reservation cases.
Explain the rule that risk prima facie passes with property (Section 26) and its exceptions.
State the rule nemo dat quod non habet and its exceptions (Sections 27 to 30 and others).
Explain the duties of seller and buyer and the rules of delivery, acceptance and rejection (Sections 31 to 44), and solve related problems.

meta.exam_tip: Problems ask "who bears the loss?" — find when property passed (Sections 20–24), then apply Section 26. For title questions, state Section 27 and test the right exception, especially good faith and notice.

concepts.title: Passing of property in specific and ascertained goods (Sections 18 to 22)
body: Why it matters: whoever has the property (ownership) normally carries the risk, can sue for the goods, and is affected by the other party's insolvency.
Section 18: in a contract for unascertained goods, no property passes until the goods are ascertained — you cannot own "500 kg out of a heap".

Section 19: for specific or ascertained goods, property passes when the parties intend it to pass. To find that intention, look at what the contract says, how the parties behaved and the surrounding facts. Sections 20 to 24 are rules to find that intention when the parties have not stated it.
Section 20: unconditional contract + specific goods + deliverable state → property passes the moment the contract is made, even if payment, delivery or both are postponed.
Section 21: if the seller must do something to put specific goods into a deliverable state (repair, assemble, pack), property passes only when it is done and the buyer is informed.
Section 22: if the goods are deliverable but the seller must weigh, measure or test them to work out the price, property passes only after that is done and the buyer is informed.

blocks.title: When does property pass? (Sections 18 to 25)

concepts.analogy: Section 20 is buying a ready cake at the counter — it is yours though you collect it tomorrow. Section 21 is a cake still to be iced — not yours until iced and you are told. Section 22 is a cake priced by weight — not yours until weighed and you are told the price.
concepts.work: Cut-off testing at the year end is an application of Sections 20 to 22: goods sold but awaiting fitting, weighing or testing usually still belong to the seller.

concepts.title: Unascertained goods, approval and right of disposal (Sections 23 to 25)
body: Section 23(1) — appropriation: where unascertained or future goods are sold by description, property passes when goods of that description, in a deliverable state, are unconditionally appropriated to the contract — by the seller with the buyer's assent or by the buyer with the seller's assent. Assent may be express or implied and may come before or after the appropriation.

Section 23(2) — delivery to carrier: if, in performing the contract, the seller hands over the goods for transmission to the buyer — to the buyer himself, or to a carrier or other bailee, named by the buyer or not — without reserving the right of disposal, he is taken to have unconditionally appropriated them.

Section 24 — goods on approval or "sale or return": property passes when the buyer (a) signifies approval or acceptance, or does any other act adopting the transaction (for example, sells or pledges the goods); or (b) keeps the goods without giving notice of rejection beyond the time fixed for return, or beyond a reasonable time if none is fixed. But if the terms say the goods remain the seller's until paid for, property passes only on payment.

Section 25 — reservation of right of disposal: the seller of specific or appropriated goods may reserve the right to dispose of them until conditions (normally payment) are met; property does not pass until then even if the goods are with the buyer or a carrier. A bill of lading taken to the seller's own order is, prima facie, a reservation. Where the seller sends a bill of exchange with the bill of lading, the buyer who does not honour the bill of exchange gets no property by keeping the bill of lading.
concepts.analogy: Sale or return is like taking clothes home "on trial": they become yours if you keep the tags off and wear them, or keep them past the return date.
concepts.work: Jewellers, publishers and FMCG firms send goods "on approval" or "on sale or return". At year end, the auditor checks which of these have been approved or kept past the return date — only those are sales.

concepts.title: Risk prima facie passes with property (Section 26)
body: Unless otherwise agreed, goods stay at the seller's risk until property passes to the buyer; once property passes, they are at the buyer's risk whether or not delivery has been made. In short: risk follows ownership, not possession.

Exceptions: (1) the parties may agree otherwise; (2) where delivery is delayed through the fault of either party, the goods are at the risk of the party at fault as regards any loss that might not have occurred but for that fault; (3) the duties of a seller or buyer as bailee of the goods for the other remain — a party holding the other's goods must take reasonable care of them.
concepts.analogy: Risk travels in the same car as ownership, not in the delivery van.
concepts.work: Insurance cover and claims in transit or warehouse fires hinge on who had the risk under Section 26 — CAs check this before booking an insurance claim receivable.

concepts.title: Transfer of title by non-owners (Sections 27 to 30)
body: Section 27 states the rule nemo dat quod non habet — a person cannot pass on a title he does not himself hold. A buyer from a person who is not the owner, and who does not sell with the owner's authority or consent, gets no better title than the seller had.
The rule protects owners; the exceptions protect honest buyers and trade. In each exception the buyer must have acted in good faith and, usually, without notice of the defect.

blocks.title: Who can give a better title than he has?

concepts.analogy: You cannot give away a gift you were never given — except where the law steps in to protect an innocent person who trusted the appearance of ownership.
concepts.work: Before a client buys second-hand vehicles or equipment, a CA verifies the seller's title (registration, invoices, charges). Most of the exceptions need good faith — documented checks are evidence of it.

concepts.title: Performance: duties and rules of delivery (Sections 31 to 36)
body: Section 31: the seller must deliver the goods and the buyer must accept and pay for them, according to the contract. Section 32: unless otherwise agreed, delivery and payment are concurrent conditions — the seller must be ready and willing to give possession in exchange for the price, and the buyer ready and willing to pay in exchange for possession.
Section 33: any act the parties have agreed to treat as delivery, or any act that gives the buyer (or a person authorised to hold for him) possession of the goods, is delivery.

Section 34: delivery of part of the goods, in progress of delivery of the whole, has the same effect as delivery of the whole for passing property; but part delivery with intention of separating that part does not count as delivery of the rest.
Section 35: unless otherwise agreed, the seller need not deliver until the buyer applies for delivery.

Section 36: (1) place — as agreed; if not, where the goods are at the time of sale (or, for goods to be made or acquired, where they are made or produced); (2) time — if the seller must send the goods and no time is fixed, within a reasonable time; (3) goods held by a third party — delivery takes place only when that person confirms to the buyer that he now holds the goods for the buyer (attornment); (4) demand or tender of delivery must be at a reasonable hour; (5) unless agreed otherwise, the seller bears the cost of putting the goods into a deliverable state.
concepts.analogy: Section 32 is like an exchange at a counter: the cashier holds out the parcel, you hold out the money — neither has to let go first.
concepts.work: Contract terms like Ex-works, FOR destination or CIF fix the place, time and cost of delivery that Section 36 would otherwise supply — CAs read them to decide when revenue and risk transfer.

concepts.title: Wrong quantity, instalments, carriers, examination (Sections 37 to 41)
body: Section 37 — wrong quantity: (1) less than contracted — buyer may reject; if he accepts, he pays at the contract rate. (2) more than contracted — buyer may accept the contracted quantity and reject the rest, or reject the whole; if he accepts the whole, he pays for it at the contract rate. (3) contracted goods mixed with goods of a different description — buyer may accept the conforming goods and reject the rest, or reject the whole. (4) All this is subject to trade usage, special agreement or course of dealing.

Section 38 — instalments: a buyer need not take delivery in parts unless the contract allows it. Where the contract provides for instalments, the effect of a defective instalment depends on the terms and the circumstances (whether the breach repudiates the whole contract or is severable).

Section 39 — delivery to a carrier for sending to the buyer is prima facie delivery to the buyer. The seller must make a reasonable contract with the carrier; and where goods go by sea in circumstances where insurance is usual, he must inform the buyer in time to insure.
Section 40 — where the seller agrees to deliver at his own risk at a distant place, the buyer still bears the risk of deterioration necessarily incidental to the course of transit.

Section 41 — a buyer who has not previously examined the goods is not deemed to have accepted them until he has had a reasonable opportunity to examine them; the seller must, on request, afford such an opportunity.
concepts.analogy: Section 37 is a waiter bringing six samosas when you ordered four: send back two, send back all, or keep all and pay for six at the menu price.
concepts.work: Goods-received notes and quantity variances are everyday matters in purchase audits; Section 37 tells the client what it may reject and what it must pay for.

concepts.title: Acceptance and its consequences (Sections 42 to 44)
body: Section 42 — the buyer is deemed to have accepted the goods when he (a) tells the seller he has accepted them; (b) after delivery, does an act in relation to the goods inconsistent with the seller's ownership (uses, resells, alters them); or (c) keeps them beyond a reasonable time without telling the seller that he rejects them.
Section 43 — a buyer who rightfully refuses delivered goods need not return them; it is enough to inform the seller of his refusal.

Section 44 — if the seller, being ready and willing, calls on the buyer to collect the goods and the buyer fails to collect within a reasonable time, the buyer must make good the loss flowing from his neglect or refusal and also pay a fair amount for looking after and storing the goods. The seller's rights where the refusal amounts to repudiation are not affected.
concepts.analogy: Using the phone you said you would "think about" is accepting it; you cannot later say you were still deciding.
concepts.work: When a customer delays lifting goods, the CA in industry raises a Section 44 claim — storage, insurance and any loss on price fall — and books it only when recovery is probable.

illustrations.title: Specific goods destroyed after the contract (Section 20 + 26)
illustrations.q: On Monday, Farah selects a particular finished teak sofa set displayed at Woodcraft and signs an unconditional order for ₹1,85,000; payment is to be made on delivery, fixed for Friday. On Wednesday night, an electrical fire (no negligence by Woodcraft) destroys the showroom and the sofa set. Who bears the loss?

solution.provision: Section 20: in an unconditional contract for specific goods in a deliverable state, property passes when the contract is made, even if payment and delivery are postponed. Section 26: unless otherwise agreed, risk passes with property, whether delivery has been made or not.
solution.facts: The sofa set was identified (specific), finished (deliverable) and the order was unconditional. Only payment and delivery were postponed to Friday. It was destroyed on Wednesday without the seller's fault.
solution.analysis: Property passed on Monday when the contract was made; risk passed with it. Woodcraft held the sofa only as a bailee and was not negligent.
solution.conclusion: Farah bears the loss and remains liable to pay ₹1,85,000.

illustrations.title: Goods to be weighed before the price is known (Section 22)
illustrations.q: Bansal agrees to buy "the entire stock of copper scrap lying in yard no. 3" from Metro Metals at ₹720 per kg. The scrap is ready for removal but has to be weighed by Metro Metals to find the price. Before weighing, the scrap is stolen in a night burglary without Metro's negligence. Metro Metals claims the price on an estimated weight. Decide.

solution.provision: Section 22: where specific goods in a deliverable state are sold but the seller is bound to weigh, measure or test them to ascertain the price, property does not pass until that is done and the buyer has notice. Section 26: risk follows property.
solution.facts: The scrap was specific (the whole stock in yard no. 3) and ready for removal, but the seller had to weigh it to fix the price. It was stolen before weighing.
solution.analysis: Since weighing had not been done, property had not passed to Bansal, and the risk remained with Metro Metals.
solution.conclusion: Metro Metals bears the loss and cannot claim the price from Bansal.

illustrations.title: Sale or return — pledging the goods (Section 24)
illustrations.q: Kundan Jewellers delivers a diamond necklace worth ₹4,60,000 to Rhea "on sale or return within 7 days". On day 3 Rhea pledges the necklace with a moneylender, Mr. Sethi, for a loan. Kundan wants the necklace back from Mr. Sethi. Advise.

solution.provision: Section 24(a): when goods are delivered on approval or on sale or return, property passes to the buyer when he signifies approval or does any other act adopting the transaction.
solution.facts: The necklace was delivered on sale or return. Within the return period, Rhea pledged it with Mr. Sethi.
solution.analysis: Pledging the necklace is an act inconsistent with merely holding it on trial; it adopts the transaction. Property passed to Rhea at that moment, so she could create a valid pledge. (The terms did not say that ownership would stay with the seller until payment.)
solution.conclusion: Mr. Sethi holds a valid pledge. Kundan cannot recover the necklace from him; its remedy is to sue Rhea for the price of ₹4,60,000.

illustrations.title: Delivery of the wrong quantity (Section 37)
illustrations.q: Prime Retail orders 500 cartons of juice at ₹640 per carton. (a) The supplier delivers 560 cartons. (b) In another month, it delivers only 450 cartons. State Prime Retail's options and the amount payable in each case.

solution.text: Section 37(2): where a larger quantity is delivered, the buyer may accept the contracted quantity and reject the rest, or reject the whole; if he accepts the whole, he pays at the contract rate. Section 37(1): where a smaller quantity is delivered, the buyer may reject; if he accepts, he pays at the contract rate.

solution.text: Working: 500 × 640 = 3,20,000; 560 × 640 = 3,58,400; 450 × 640 = 2,88,000. All at the contract rate — the buyer cannot be charged more per carton for extra goods.

illustrations.title: Seller in possession sells twice (Section 30(1))
illustrations.q: On 2 May, Sameer sells his used tractor to Dhruv for ₹5,20,000 and receives payment. Dhruv asks Sameer to keep the tractor in his shed for a week. On 5 May Sameer sells and delivers the same tractor to Komal for ₹5,40,000; Komal knows nothing of the earlier sale. Dhruv claims the tractor from Komal. Decide.

solution.provision: Section 27: a buyer generally gets no better title than his seller. Section 30(1): if a seller who has already sold goods stays in possession of them and then sells or pledges and delivers them (himself or through a mercantile agent) to someone who takes them honestly and unaware of the first sale, that transfer is as effective as if the owner had authorised it.
solution.facts: Property passed to Dhruv on 2 May (specific goods, unconditional sale). Sameer stayed in possession and on 5 May sold and delivered the tractor to Komal, who acted in good faith without notice.
solution.analysis: Although Sameer was no longer the owner, he was a seller in possession. Komal took delivery in good faith without notice, so the exception in Section 30(1) applies.
solution.conclusion: Komal gets a good title. Dhruv cannot recover the tractor from her; he can sue Sameer for damages / refund of ₹5,20,000.

illustrations.title: Buyer delays taking delivery (Section 44)
illustrations.q: Annapurna Mills is ready to deliver 120 bags of flour to Hotel Sunrise at ₹2,400 a bag and asks the hotel to collect them on 1 October. The hotel collects them only after 18 days, without any valid reason. A reasonable storage charge is ₹1,500 per day. Because of the delay the mill also had to forgo a resale opportunity and its loss from the fall in price is ₹120 a bag. What can the mill recover besides the price?

solution.provision: Section 44: a buyer who, despite a request from a seller ready and willing to deliver, fails to take delivery within a reasonable time is answerable for the loss his neglect or refusal causes, plus a fair charge for keeping the goods safe.
solution.facts: The mill was ready and asked the hotel to collect on 1 October. The hotel delayed 18 days without reason. Storage costs ₹1,500 a day and the delay caused a loss of ₹120 a bag.
solution.analysis: Both heads are recoverable under Section 44: custody charges and the loss occasioned by the delay.
solution.conclusion: Besides the price, the mill can recover ₹41,400.

head: Head
Amount (₹)
rows: Care and custody: 18 days × ₹1,500
Loss caused by delay: 120 bags × ₹120
Total recoverable

checks.label: reasonable charge for care and custody: 18 days × 1,500
loss from price fall caused by the delay: 120 bags × 120

jobs.title: Goods "on approval" at the year end
jobs.role: Audit senior at a publishing house
jobs.situation: Books worth ₹42 lakh were sent to bookshops on "sale or return within 60 days" during February and March. The client has booked all of them as sales in March.
steps: List the consignments with dates, return periods and any approvals received.
Apply Section 24: property (and therefore a sale) arises only on approval, an act adopting the sale, or expiry of the return period without rejection.
Consignments still within the 60-day window at 31 March without approval are not sales; reverse them and include the books in closing stock at cost.
jobs.takeaway: For sale-or-return goods the sale date is decided by Section 24, not by the despatch date.
jobs.think: A bookshop sold some of the books to its customers in March but had not "approved" anything in writing. Has property passed for those books?
jobs.answer: Yes. Reselling the books is an act adopting the transaction under Section 24(a), so property passed to the bookshop when it resold them.

jobs.title: Buying vehicles from a dealer — checking title
jobs.role: CA in industry, procurement head of a logistics company
jobs.situation: A dealer offers ten used trucks at an attractive price. Two of them appear to be under hire purchase with a bank.
steps: Recall nemo dat (Section 27): a hirer is not the owner, so a buyer from him generally gets no title.
Search the vehicle registration and hypothecation records, and ask for no-objection certificates from the financiers.
Obtain an indemnity and keep evidence of good faith; buy the two vehicles only after the financier releases them.
jobs.takeaway: Documented title checks protect the client — and good faith is the key to most exceptions anyway.

jobs.title: Delivery to the carrier and transit losses
jobs.role: Accounts manager of an e-commerce seller
jobs.situation: Goods sent through a courier to a business buyer were lost in transit. The buyer refuses to pay.
steps: Check the contract terms: who bears transit risk? If silent, delivery to the carrier for sending to the buyer is prima facie delivery to the buyer (Section 39(1)), and unconditional appropriation passes property (Section 23(2)).
Check whether the seller made a reasonable contract with the courier (Section 39(2)); if not, the buyer may refuse to treat it as delivery.
Decide whether to pursue the buyer for the price or lodge an insurance/courier claim, and record the receivable accordingly.
jobs.takeaway: Unless the contract says otherwise, risk in transit usually sits with the buyer once the seller properly hands the goods to the carrier.

mcqs.q: In a contract for the sale of unascertained goods, property passes:
options: Only after the goods are ascertained
mcqs.explain: Section 18: in a contract for unascertained goods, no property passes until the goods are ascertained, that is, picked out and identified as the goods of this contract. Until then nobody can say which units belong to the buyer. "When the contract is made" is the trap: that rule (Section 20) applies only to specific goods in a deliverable state. Paying the price does not by itself identify any goods. In practice: when a buyer orders 100 tonnes of steel from a mill's general stock, the mill keeps owning it until particular coils are tagged and set aside for him.
mcqs.topic: Risk Prima Facie Passes with Property (Section 26)

mcqs.q: Specific goods in a deliverable state are sold under an unconditional contract; delivery and payment are postponed. Property passes:
mcqs.explain: Section 20: where there is an unconditional contract for specific goods in a deliverable state, property passes when the contract is made. It does not matter that payment, delivery or both are postponed. "On delivery" is the trap: under the Sale of Goods Act, ownership can pass before the buyer takes possession. Because risk follows property, the buyer bears the risk from the date of the contract. In practice: a buyer who signs for a specific, ready car in a showroom and collects it a week later should insure it from the signing date.
mcqs.topic: Risk Prima Facie Passes with Property (Section 26)

mcqs.q: Where the seller must weigh specific goods to ascertain the price, property passes when:
options: The goods are weighed and the buyer has notice of it
mcqs.explain: Section 22: where the seller must weigh, measure or test specific goods to fix the price, property does not pass until that act is done and the buyer has notice that it has been done. Both steps are needed. "When the goods are weighed" is the trap, because it leaves out the notice to the buyer. Payment is not the deciding event. In practice: in a sale of a specific heap of cotton priced per quintal, the ginning unit weighs it and sends the weighment slip to the buyer, and only then does ownership move.
mcqs.topic: Risk Prima Facie Passes with Property (Section 26)

mcqs.q: Goods are sent on "sale or return" and no time is fixed for return. The buyer keeps them without giving notice of rejection. Property passes:
options: On expiry of a reasonable time
mcqs.explain: Section 24(b): when goods are sent on approval or "sale or return", and the buyer keeps them without giving notice of rejection, property passes when the fixed time ends; if no time is fixed, when a reasonable time ends. "Immediately on delivery" is the trap: on sale or return, delivery alone never makes the buyer owner. The law fixes no 30-day period. In practice: publishers and garment suppliers who send stock to retailers on sale or return set a clear return date in the delivery challan, so ownership and revenue are not left uncertain.
mcqs.topic: Risk Prima Facie Passes with Property (Section 26)

mcqs.q: A bill of lading taken out to the order of the seller indicates that the seller has prima facie:
mcqs.explain: Section 25(2): where goods are shipped and the bill of lading makes them deliverable to the seller's (or his agent's) order, the seller is presumed, unless shown otherwise, to have reserved the right of disposal. Property therefore does not pass merely because the goods are shipped. "Transferred property to the buyer" is the trap: shipment by itself is not unconditional appropriation here. In practice: exporters take bills of lading "to order" and send them through banks, releasing them to the importer only on payment or acceptance of the bill.
mcqs.topic: Risk Prima Facie Passes with Property (Section 26)

options: With the property in the goods
mcqs.explain: Section 26: unless otherwise agreed, goods remain at the seller's risk until property passes to the buyer, and after that they are at the buyer's risk, whether or not delivery has been made. "With possession" is the trap: a buyer may own goods still lying with the seller and must bear their loss. Payment and the invoice do not decide risk. In practice: auditors and insurers look at when ownership passed, not who holds the goods, to decide who bears a fire loss at year-end.
mcqs.topic: Risk Prima Facie Passes with Property (Section 26)

mcqs.q: Delivery is delayed through the buyer's fault and the goods are damaged in the meantime. The loss caused by the delay falls on:
mcqs.explain: The proviso to Section 26 says that where delivery is delayed through the fault of either party, the goods are at that party's risk for any loss that might not have happened but for the fault. Here the buyer caused the delay, so the buyer bears the loss caused by the delay. "The seller", because he still holds the goods, is the trap. In practice: suppliers send a written notice when the goods are ready and the buyer fails to collect, so that storage loss or damage can later be charged to the buyer.
mcqs.topic: Risk Prima Facie Passes with Property (Section 26)

options: No one can give what he does not have
mcqs.explain: Nemo dat quod non habet means "no one can give what he does not have". Section 27 applies it: a buyer from a person who is not the owner, and who sells without the owner's authority, usually gets no better title than the seller had. "Let the buyer beware" is the trap: that is caveat emptor, a rule about quality. Sections 27 to 30 list the exceptions. In practice: a dealer who unknowingly buys a stolen motorcycle must return it to the true owner and can only sue the thief for his money.

mcqs.q: A buyer in good faith gets a good title from a person who obtained the goods under a voidable contract, provided:
options: The contract had not been rescinded at the time of sale
The contract had already been rescinded
The buyer paid more than market price
The seller was a mercantile agent
mcqs.explain: Section 29: a person who obtains goods under a contract voidable for fraud, coercion and the like can still pass good title to a buyer in good faith, as long as the contract had not been rescinded when he resold. Choosing "already rescinded" is the trap: once the original owner rescinds, the seller has nothing left to pass. Price paid is irrelevant, and the seller need not be a mercantile agent. In practice: a victim of a cheque fraud should rescind quickly, for instance by complaining to the police, before the goods are resold.

mcqs.q: Unless otherwise agreed, delivery of goods and payment of price are:
options: Conditions precedent for the seller only
mcqs.explain: Section 32: unless the parties agree differently, handing over the goods and paying the price are concurrent conditions. The seller must be ready to deliver against payment, and the buyer must be ready to pay against delivery. "Independent promises" is the trap: they are linked, so neither side can insist on performance by the other while refusing its own. In practice: cash-on-delivery sales are concurrent conditions in action, as the courier hands over the parcel only when the buyer pays.
mcqs.topic: Performance of the Contract of Sale (Sections 31 – 44)

mcqs.q: A buyer ordered 200 units at ₹150 each; 240 are delivered and he decides to keep all of them. He must pay:
mcqs.explain: Section 37(2): when a larger quantity than ordered is delivered, the buyer may accept the contracted quantity, reject the whole, or accept everything. If he keeps all of it, he pays at the contract rate: 240 × ₹150 = ₹36,000. ₹30,000 is the trap: it pays for the 200 ordered units only, though he kept 240. ₹6,000 is the price of the 40 extra units alone. In practice: stores teams check delivered quantity against the purchase order, and accounts pass the bill for the extra units only if the purchase manager approves keeping them.
mcqs.topic: Performance of the Contract of Sale (Sections 31 – 44)

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT a way in which the buyer is deemed to accept goods under Section 42?
options: He receives the goods and promptly informs the seller that he rejects them
He tells the seller he has accepted them
He resells the goods after delivery
He keeps the goods beyond a reasonable time without intimating rejection
mcqs.explain: Section 42 deems acceptance when the buyer tells the seller he accepts, does an act inconsistent with the seller's ownership such as reselling, or keeps the goods beyond a reasonable time without saying he rejects them. Promptly telling the seller of rejection is the opposite of acceptance. Section 43 adds that he need not even send the goods back. Long silence is the trap: it is deemed acceptance. In practice: purchase teams send rejection notes quickly, because silence beyond a reasonable time locks the company into paying.
mcqs.topic: Performance of the Contract of Sale (Sections 31 – 44)

questions.q: "A buyer cannot acquire a better title than the seller had." Explain this rule and state the exceptions to it under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930.

model.text: Rule — Section 27 (nemo dat quod non habet): where goods are sold by a person who is not their owner and who does not sell with the authority or consent of the owner, the buyer gets no better title than the seller had, unless the owner is precluded by his conduct from denying the seller's authority.
Exceptions (the honest buyer gets a good title):

items: Estoppel — the owner by conduct led the buyer to believe the seller had authority (Section 27).

Mercantile agent — in possession of the goods or documents with the owner's consent, selling in the ordinary course of business, to a buyer in good faith without notice of want of authority (Section 27 proviso).
Joint owner in sole possession with the others' permission — buyer in good faith without notice (Section 28).
Seller holding under a voidable contract not rescinded at the time of sale — buyer in good faith without notice (Section 29).
Seller continuing in possession after sale — delivery to a good-faith buyer without notice of the earlier sale (Section 30(1)).
Buyer in possession with the seller's consent before property passes — resale to a good-faith buyer without notice (Section 30(2)).
Unpaid seller who resells after exercising lien or stoppage in transit (Section 54(3)).
Sales under other laws — finder of goods (Contract Act s. 169), pawnee (s. 176), official receiver, liquidator or court officer.

questions.q: Sunrise Electronics delivers 10 air-conditioners to Cool Homes "on approval; to be returned within 15 days if not approved". Cool Homes neither approves nor rejects them, and still has them on day 25. Meanwhile 3 units are stolen from its warehouse on day 20. Who bears the loss of the stolen units, and what must Cool Homes pay if each unit is priced at ₹38,000?

model.provision: Section 24(b): where goods are delivered on approval or sale or return and the buyer retains them without giving notice of rejection, property passes on expiry of the time fixed for return. Section 26: risk passes with property.

model.analysis: Property in all 10 units passed to Cool Homes on expiry of 15 days. On day 20 the goods were at its risk.

questions.q: State the rules regarding delivery of the wrong quantity of goods under Section 37 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930.

items: Short delivery — the buyer may reject the goods; if he accepts them, he must pay at the contract rate [Section 37(1)].
Excess delivery — the buyer may (i) accept the contracted quantity and reject the excess, (ii) reject the whole, or (iii) accept the whole and pay for it at the contract rate [Section 37(2)].
Mixed delivery — where contracted goods are mixed with goods of a different description, the buyer may accept the goods that conform and reject the rest, or reject the whole [Section 37(3)].
All of the above give way to a trade custom, a special agreement or the past course of dealing of the parties [Section 37(4)].

questions.q: Explain any six rules regarding delivery of goods under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930.

items: Mode (Section 33): anything agreed as delivery, or which puts the goods in the possession of the buyer or his authorised agent.
Delivery and payment are concurrent conditions unless otherwise agreed (Section 32).
Part delivery in progress of delivery of the whole operates as delivery of the whole for passing property, unless intended to sever that part (Section 34).
The seller is not bound to deliver until the buyer applies for delivery (Section 35).
Place: as agreed, else where the goods are at the time of sale; time: if seller must send, within a reasonable time (Section 36(1), (2)).
Goods held by a third party: delivery only when he acknowledges to the buyer that he holds on the buyer's behalf (Section 36(3)).
Demand or tender at a reasonable hour; expenses of putting goods into a deliverable state borne by the seller (Section 36(4), (5)).

Buyer not bound to accept instalments (Section 38); delivery to a carrier is prima facie delivery to the buyer (Section 39); buyer bears deterioration necessarily incidental to transit (Section 40); right to examine (Section 41).

summary: Unascertained goods: no property until ascertained (18). Specific goods: when intended (19) — rules in 20 to 24.
20: deliverable + unconditional → at contract. 21: seller to make deliverable → when done + notice. 22: seller to weigh/measure/test → when done + notice.

23: unconditional appropriation with assent; delivery to carrier without reserving disposal = appropriation. 24: approval/adoption/retention beyond time. 25: right of disposal reserved → passes on conditions.
26: risk follows property; exceptions — agreement, delay by fault, bailee's duties.
27: nemo dat; exceptions — mercantile agent, estoppel, joint owner (28), voidable contract (29), seller/buyer in possession (30), unpaid seller (54(3)), other laws.

31–36: duties, concurrent conditions, modes, part delivery, buyer to apply, place/time/third party/hour/expenses. 37–41: wrong quantity, instalments, carrier, transit deterioration, examination. 42–44: acceptance, no duty to return rejected goods, liability for neglecting delivery.
remember: Sections 21 and 22 need the act done AND notice to the buyer.
Section 37: extra goods accepted are paid at the contract rate.
Section 43: rightful rejection — just notify, no need to return.
traps: In Section 29 the contract must NOT have been rescinded at the time of sale.
Sale or return with "property till paid" clause: adoption alone does not pass property.
Delivery to a carrier is only prima facie delivery to the buyer — reserved right of disposal changes it.

viva.q: What is the rule as to passing of risk, and what are its exceptions?

cases.title: Silk sarees on sale or return
cases.case: Kanchi Weavers sent 12 silk sarees, priced at ₹7,500 each, to Trends Boutique on 1 March "on sale or return within 10 days". On 4 March the boutique sold 4 sarees to its customers. On 8 March it returned 3 sarees with a note rejecting them. It kept the remaining 5 sarees without saying anything until 25 March, when it tried to return them. Kanchi Weavers refused to take them back.

mcqs.q: When did property in the 4 sarees sold to customers pass to Trends Boutique?
options: On 4 March, when it resold them
On 11 March, on expiry of 10 days
Never — goods on approval never become the buyer's
mcqs.explain: Section 24(a): on sale or return, property passes when the buyer tells the seller he approves, or does any other act adopting the transaction. Reselling the sarees to customers on 4 March is plainly such an act, so ownership of those 4 passed on 4 March. "1 March, on delivery" is the trap: delivery on approval does not pass ownership. The 10-day limit matters only for sarees not dealt with. In practice: consignment retailers record the purchase on the day they sell to a customer, which matches Section 24(a).
mcqs.topic: Risk Prima Facie Passes with Property (Section 26)

mcqs.q: Is Kanchi Weavers bound to take back the 5 sarees on 25 March?
options: No — property passed when the 10 days expired without notice of rejection
Yes — the boutique never approved them
Yes — goods on sale or return can be returned at any time
No — because the boutique sold some other sarees
mcqs.explain: Section 24(b): where a time is fixed for return and the buyer keeps the goods beyond it without giving notice of rejection, property passes when that time ends. The boutique kept 5 sarees past 11 March without a word, so they became its property, and it cannot return them on 25 March. "Can be returned at any time" is the trap: the fixed period sets the limit. In practice: suppliers on sale or return track the expiry of each approval period and invoice automatically on the next day.
mcqs.topic: Risk Prima Facie Passes with Property (Section 26)

mcqs.q: How much must Trends Boutique pay Kanchi Weavers in all?
mcqs.explain: The boutique pays for every saree whose property passed: 4 resold + 5 kept beyond 10 days = 9 sarees × ₹7,500 = ₹67,500. The 3 returned with notice within the period are not paid for. ₹90,000 is the trap: it charges all 12 sarees sent, including the 3 properly rejected. ₹37,500 counts only the 5 retained sarees. In practice: at month-end a CA reconciles a supplier's sale-or-return statement this way, counting goods sold, goods held past the deadline and goods returned.
mcqs.topic: Risk Prima Facie Passes with Property (Section 26)

mcqs.q: Had the delivery note said "sarees remain the property of Kanchi Weavers until paid for", the 4 sarees sold to customers on 4 March would have:
options: Remained Kanchi's property until payment, the boutique not having become owner first
Become the customers' automatically as the boutique was the owner
Been treated as a hire purchase
mcqs.explain: Section 24 is subject to the terms of the contract. If the note says the sarees remain Kanchi's property until paid for, adoption by resale does not pass ownership to the boutique; property passes only when the condition, payment, is met. "Become the boutique's on delivery" is the trap: retention of ownership overrides the default rule. Whether customers get good title then depends on nemo dat exceptions such as Section 30(2). In practice: suppliers print a "retention of title" clause on invoices to protect themselves if the retailer fails.
mcqs.topic: Risk Prima Facie Passes with Property (Section 26)
